In modern Tamil film scoring and contemporary tracks—particularly fast-tempo dance tracks—the music director composes the tune and percussive track first as a "meter" (or Mattu), which is then passed to the lyricist to fill with words that fit the exact syllabic pulse.

1. Meter-First Composition (Metthuku Paattu) When a track relies heavily on short-burst cadence (such as "Lighta vaangude," "Lighta kekkude," "Rafana man," "Tappana girl"), the music composer sets the rhythmic framework (tala and groove) using dummy syllables or rhythm markers (Thillana or beat counts). The lyrics are drafted to match that precise tempo.

2. Anglophonic & Phonetic Fitting Because modern beat patterns often use syncopated percussive hits, traditional pure Tamil words—which can carry longer, multi-syllabic stress patterns—do not always fit the quick-fire rhythm. Anglophonic and Tanglish words ("Lighta," "Girl," "Man") act as phonetic "fillers" or shock-absorbers. English loanwords provide sharp, single-syllable consonant stops (like t, k, p) that naturally sync up with snare hits and electronic beats.

3. The Dravidian-Anglophonic Hybridization Tanglish balances the grounding of local dialect with the energetic, staccato flow of global pop/hip-hop. Blending Dravidian phonetic flexibility with English vocabulary allows the lyricist to play with sound textures rather than strict grammatical rules, creating catchier hook lines that adapt seamlessly to the beat track.

The track's rhythmic backbone was produced first, with the Tanglish lyrics explicitly engineered afterward to lock into the beat.
